extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, patent practitioners, examiners, and advanced law students (U.S. reissue/amendment practice)
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards governing when and how U.S. patents may be amended by surrender-and-reissue (including divisional reissues), limits on changes, timing/laches, and the legal effect of surrender and reissue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Described-but-unclaimed matters in use cannot be claimed after unreasonable delay
rubrics_metrics.description: Where matters have been described but not claimed in the original patent, and have gone into use by others, they cannot be claimed in a re-issue after unreasonable delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an inventor described subject matter in the specification but omitted it from the claims, and third parties have used that matter, the inventor may be barred from later claiming it by reissue if there has been an unreasonable delay. (Cases cited: Wooster v. Handy, Brainard v. Cramme, etc.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice from pre‑filing use of 'new matter' and effect on reissue
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of the 'new matter' before the original application was filed gives sufficient notice of the defect to make continued acquiescence a conclusive admission that the original patent represented the entire invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the patentee had constructive or actual notice of omitted subject matter (e.g., because the matter was in use before filing), failure to amend within a reasonable time may be treated as acquiescence and bar reissue. Courts determine what is reasonable from the facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intentional exclusion not inferred from mere delay
rubrics_metrics.description: An intention to exclude from the original patent the patentable matter suggested in its description but omitted from its claims is never inferred from mere delay alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delay by itself does not establish that the inventor intentionally omitted subject matter. Other evidence of intent or prejudice to others is required before denying reissue on that basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment for inadvertence/mistake allowed if no new matter introduced
rubrics_metrics.description: The amendment of defects occurring through accident, mistake, or inadvertence, and without fraud, may be made at any time when the error is discovered or the amendment becomes desirable, provided the amendment does not introduce into the patent any invention not substantially indicated by the original specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts generally give liberality to patentees to correct inadvertent errors, but will bar amendments that would introduce new patentable subject matter not present in the original disclosure. Avoidable delay can defeat the right to reissue.

rubrics_metrics.name: No fixed statute of limitation; 'reasonable time' standard governs delay
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no precise limit of time for applying for reissue; the amendment must be made within a 'reasonable time' determined by the courts from all circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex specifications and ambiguous claims may justify greater indulgence. Courts assess whether delay was avoidable and whether it prejudiced others; unreasonably long or avoidable delay can preclude reissue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissue may be made in any form necessary to secure the actual invention
rubrics_metrics.description: When an amendment by reissue is allowable it can be made in any form and to any extent necessary to render the patent effective for the original invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The language of the specification can be varied indefinitely; new claims may be added or old claims divided and restated to achieve protection for the invention, so long as no new matter is introduced that was absent from the original description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissue must not introduce patentable matter absent from original description
rubrics_metrics.description: New patentable matter not substantially indicated by the original specification may not be introduced by reissue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reissue cannot be used to claim an invention that was not present in the original disclosure (in fact and function). Such additions render the reissue invalid to the extent they introduce new matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: New claims may be added from the old specification if omission was by mistake and patentee not estopped
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issue may contain new claims based on the old specification if such claims were omitted by mistake and the patentee has not been estopped from amending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts allow adding claims that were present in the original disclosure but omitted by mistake, provided there has been no estoppel or prejudice to others; citations include Combined Patents Co. v. Lloyd and Swift v. Whisen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissue cannot change the invention by narrowing one claim and expanding another
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issue cannot change the invention by narrowing a claim in one part and expanding it in another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reissue must be consistent overall; selectively narrowing and expanding can amount to changing the invention and render the reissue improper. (Gage v. Kellogg cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Unwarranted expansion of claims in reissue is void
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issue that unwarrantably expands the claims is void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attempting to broaden claim scope beyond what the original patent permitted (especially to cover prior art or third‑party use) will invalidate the reissue or the expanded claims. (Uoe v. Knap and others.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Original cannot be broadened to include matter anticipated by prior devices
rubrics_metrics.description: The original patent cannot be broadened by re-issue so as to include matter anticipated by prior devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If broadened claims read on prior art (matter anticipated), the re-issue is improper. Courts will not permit reissue to reach subject matter anticipatory of prior devices. (Ives & Millers, Hartford Spring & Axle Co. cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Inexact reissue claims that naturally expand the invention are void
rubrics_metrics.description: An inexact claim in the re-issue which, if naturally construed, would expand the invention is void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims in the reissue must be precise and not ambiguous in a way that would enlarge the patent monopoly beyond what the original disclosure justified. (Tyler v. Galloway cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissue not granted merely to make description fuller when specs/drawings unchanged
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the specification and drawings are the same as those of the original the re-issue is not granted for making the description more full or for disclaiming old matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reissue is not to be used simply to elaborate or clarify where there is no substantive change or correction needed; such an application may be denied. (McMurray v. Mallory cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissue cannot create a new and substantially different invention or produce different effects
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issue cannot contain any change in the original specification or claim whereby a new and substantially different invention results, or different effects are produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claimed changes would result in a different inventive concept or new operative effects, the reissue is invalid. (Salamander Felting Co. v. Haven cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Single original patent may reissue in several divisions (divisional reissues allowed)
rubrics_metrics.description: A single original patent may be surrendered and re-issued in several divisions, each covering separate patentable parts of the original disclosure (e.g., combination, sub-combinations, elements; process vs. product).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Divisional reissues are permitted where the original describes multiple distinct inventions or complex combinations; divisions can be issued concurrently or successively to cover separate parts. (Giant Powder Co., Selden v. Stockwell, etc.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Divisional reissues must be confined to inventions indicated in the original specification and be patentable separately
rubrics_metrics.description: Reissue divisions must be for distinct inventions embraced in the original, not merely different applications of the same invention under the same genus; each division must claim a complete invention in itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Divisions should reflect separable, patentable subject matter that was indicated in the original disclosure; mere variants or alternative applications within the same genus do not justify separate divisional reissues. (Ex parte Herr, Ex parte Sexton, etc.)

rubrics_metrics.name: All divisions must issue to the same patentee
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the divisions of a re-issue represent a single original patent, they must be granted to the same patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Divisional reissues are tied to the original patent's ownership; they cannot be separately assigned at the time of issuance to different parties. (Ex parte Smith cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Each division judged on its own merits; incurable defects in original void all divisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Each division is judged as a separate patent for a separate invention and is not affected by errors in the others; however, an incurable defect in the original (e.g., false oath, fraudulent concealment) renders all divisions void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although divisions stand individually, they rest on the original patent as the foundation; defects that taint the original corrupt all derived divisional patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissued patent supersedes and requires surrender/cancellation of original
rubrics_metrics.description: The grant of the re-issue necessitates the previous surrender and cancellation of the original defective patent; the surrender (delivery or certified copy to PTO) extinguishes the original patent and its claims when accepted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surrender is effected by delivering the original patent (or certified copy if lost) to the Patent Office with a reissue request; once accepted, the original patent's rights are extinguished and the reissued patent is the operative grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: All rights of action under original expire with surrender and reissue; reissue gives no remedy for past infringements under void original
rubrics_metrics.description: All rights of action under the original patent are suspended or expire with surrender and reissue; the statute gives no right of action for infringements occurring under the void patent prior to reissue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patentee cannot recover damages for acts of infringement that occurred under an original patent later admitted to be invalid when the patentee has surrendered that patent and taken a reissue. Courts construe the statute to deny retrospective remedies. (Jones v. Barker, Peck v. Collins, etc.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissue operates prospectively from its date for subsequent causes of action
rubrics_metrics.description: The re-issued patent has effect and operation for causes subsequently accruing as though it had originally issued in the corrected form; it does not retroactively create remedies for prior infringing acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statute and decisions provide that the new patent is operative for subsequent infringement actions; the date of the original patent may still fix priority, but damages for prior activity under the surrendered patent are not allowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Successive reissues permitted until patent meets intended purpose, subject to limits
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee may make successive reissue attempts until the patent meets the protection intended, but successive reissues are constrained: each must be for the same invention as prior reissues, and faults of prior reissues do not necessarily preclude later correct reissues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will permit multiple reissues to correct defects, but scrutinize whether successive changes introduce new matter or unfairly enlarge scope. A second reissue must be for the same invention as the first; where a reissue is void the original may sometimes be reissued in its exact language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division and enlargement of claims in reissue is not favored but allowed if no new matter introduced
rubrics_metrics.description: Division and enlargement (division into separate claims or expansion) of claims in a re-issue is not favored, though it is allowed if no new matter is introduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts approach such changes cautiously; enlargement that reads on new subject matter or prior art will be invalid, but reorganization of claims to better reflect the original disclosure is permitted when done without adding new matter. (Dederick v. Cassell and related cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification and claims of reissue may differ in wording if they claim nothing beyond what was present in the original (in fact and function)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification and claims of the re-issue may differ from those of the original provided they claim nothing except what was present, both in fact and function, either in the original drawings or model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different language in the reissue is acceptable so long as the reissued claims are consistent with the original disclosure and do not introduce substantively new subject matter. (Stephenson v. Second Avenue R.R. Co. cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Divisional reissues may each claim the part in separate condition and in combination with others
rubrics_metrics.description: Each reissue division may claim its own part in its separate condition and also as connected with the others; one division may describe the whole invention to explain the claimed portion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Divisions should enable public understanding of the separated device's application; describing the whole machine for context is permissible, but that description does not expand what the patent actually covers beyond the claims.
